rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem: The correct order for the increasing oxidizing power in 3d series of transition elements is :
rows.solution:
Increasing oxidising power runs
\(\mathrm{VO_2^{+}} < \mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}} < \mathrm{MnO_4^{-}}\)

All three are the metal in its HIGHEST oxidation state — vanadium \(+5\), chromium \(+6\), manganese \(+7\) — and the question is which is the most anxious to come down from it.

That anxiety grows across the series. The higher the oxidation state relative to what the element holds comfortably, the less stable the species, and the more readily it accepts electrons. Permanganate at \(+7\) is the most extreme, and it is the strongest oxidising agent of the three; the vanadyl ion at \(+5\) is the mildest, vanadium holding \(+5\) quite happily.

The standard potentials bear it out: about \(+1{\cdot}0\) V for the vanadium couple, \(+1{\cdot}33\) V for dichromate and \(+1{\cdot}51\) V for permanganate.

rows.stem: The type of isomerism shown by the complex \(\mathrm{[CoCl_2(en)_2]^{+}}\) is :
rows.solution:
The complex shows GEOMETRICAL ISOMERISM.

\(\mathrm{[CoCl_2(en)_2]^{+}}\) is octahedral with two chlorido ligands and two bidentate diamines — the type \(\mathrm{MA_2(BB)_2}\). The two chlorides may sit ADJACENT, giving the CIS isomer, or OPPOSITE each other, giving the TRANS isomer.

The other three need something this complex does not have. LINKAGE isomerism needs an ambidentate ligand, and neither chloride nor the diamine is one. COORDINATION isomerism needs both the cation and the anion to be complex ions. IONISATION isomerism needs a counter ion that could swap places with a ligand, and here the counter ion is not specified in a way that permits it.

The cis form is also OPTICALLY active, having no plane of symmetry — so this complex shows optical isomerism as well, but only geometrical isomerism is offered.

rows.stem: Which one of the following hybrid states is associated with low spin complex ?
rows.solution:
A LOW SPIN complex is associated with \(d^2sp^3\) hybridisation.

Low spin means the ligand field is STRONG enough to force the d electrons to pair up, and pairing them within the lower \(t_{2g}\) set is what FREES two inner \((n-1)d\) orbitals for bonding. Those two, with the \(ns\) and the three \(np\), give \(d^2sp^3\) — an INNER ORBITAL complex, octahedral, with fewer unpaired electrons than the free ion had.

\(sp^3d^2\) is the mirror image: there the field is WEAK, no pairing occurs, no inner d orbital is free, and bonding must reach outwards to the \(nd\) set. That is the high spin, outer orbital case.

The remaining two describe different geometries altogether — \(sp^3\) tetrahedral and \(sp^3d\) trigonal bipyramidal — and the high-versus-low spin distinction is not usually applied to them.

rows.stem: Butanenitrile may be prepared by heating :
rows.solution:
Butanenitrile is prepared from PROPYL CHLORIDE with potassium cyanide.

COUNT THE CARBONS, which is what this question turns on. Butanenitrile is \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2{-}C{\equiv}N}\), four carbons in all — but one of them is the NITRILE carbon, supplied by the cyanide ion. The alkyl halide must therefore bring only THREE.

\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2Cl} + \mathrm{KCN} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2CN} + \mathrm{KCl}\)

Butyl chloride would give pentanenitrile, one carbon too many.

The two alcohols fail for a different reason: a hydroxyl group is a poor leaving group and will not be displaced by cyanide. It must first be converted to a halide or a sulphonate.

rows.stem: Which of the following is most acidic ?
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - ALL FOUR options are PRINTED AS DRAWINGS; the stem names nothing. Read at 3x zoom: (A) a KEKULE benzene ring (three inner double-bond strokes) bonded at its top vertex to the label "OH"; (B) the SAME Kekule ring bonded to the label "CH2OH"; (C) a PLAIN hexagon with NO inner strokes (i.e. a saturated six-membered ring) bonded to "OH" - this is the cyclohexanol-not-phenol distinction the corpus is known to carry, and it was verified glyph by glyph against (A) on the same page; (D) a Kekule ring with "OH" at the top vertex and "NO2" at the OPPOSITE (para) vertex. Transcribed above as lossless condensed formulae. Page idx 4.
rows.solution:
The most acidic is p-NITROPHENOL.

First separate the phenols from the alcohols. Both phenols listed are far stronger acids than either alcohol, because the phenoxide ion's negative charge is delocalised INTO THE RING by resonance, while an alkoxide's charge is stuck on one oxygen. Benzyl alcohol and cyclohexanol are ordinary alcohols, with \(\mathrm{pK_a}\) around 16.

Then compare the two phenols. The nitro group is strongly electron WITHDRAWING, and from the PARA position it withdraws by resonance as well as inductively — it can take the negative charge right onto its own oxygen. That stabilises the anion enormously, so the proton leaves far more readily: p-nitrophenol has \(\mathrm{pK_a}\) about 7.1 against phenol's 10, nearly a thousandfold difference.

Note that benzyl alcohol, despite having a ring, is NOT a phenol — its hydroxyl is on a side-chain carbon, not on the ring, so the anion gets no resonance help.

rows.stem: \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_2\,CH - O - CH_3}\) reacts with HI to give :
rows.solution:
The products are ISOPROPYL ALCOHOL AND METHYL IODIDE, \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_2CH{-}OH} + \mathrm{CH_3{-}I}\).

Here neither group is tertiary — one is secondary and one primary — so the cleavage goes by the BIMOLECULAR route. The acid protonates the ether, and the iodide then attacks the carbon it can reach most easily, which is the LESS HINDERED one.

Of a methyl group and an isopropyl group, the methyl is far the less hindered. So the iodine goes to the METHYL carbon and the isopropyl group keeps the oxygen:
\((\mathrm{CH_3})_2\mathrm{CH{-}O{-}CH_3} + \mathrm{HI} \longrightarrow (\mathrm{CH_3})_2\mathrm{CH{-}OH} + \mathrm{CH_3I}\)

The contrast with a TERTIARY ether is worth holding. There the protonated ether falls apart to a stable tertiary carbocation, the route is unimolecular, and the iodide goes to the MORE substituted carbon instead — the opposite pairing, from the same reagent.

rows.stem: A compound (X) with the molecular formula \(\mathrm{C_3H_8O}\) can be oxidized by strong oxidizing agents to another compound (Y) whose molecular formula is \(\mathrm{C_3H_6O_2}\). The compound (X) is :
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE - option (B) alone is printed as a TWO-DIMENSIONAL structure: the chain "CH3 - CH - CH3" with a vertical bond dropping from the middle carbon to an "OH" written beneath it. The linear transcription above renders that as the condensed \(\mathrm{CH_3 - CH(OH) - CH_3}\), which is faithful in identity but not in layout. Options (A), (C) and (D) are ordinary text and need no crop. Page idx 6.
rows.solution:
Compound \(\mathrm{X}\) is PROPAN-1-OL, \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2OH}\).

Compare the two formulae. Going from \(\mathrm{C_3H_8O}\) to \(\mathrm{C_3H_6O_2}\) means LOSING two hydrogens and GAINING one oxygen, with the carbon count unchanged — the signature of oxidising a primary alcohol all the way to the CARBOXYLIC ACID. The product \(\mathrm{C_3H_6O_2}\) is propanoic acid.

Only a PRIMARY alcohol does that. The secondary alcohol propan-2-ol would be oxidised to propanone, \(\mathrm{C_3H_6O}\) — one oxygen short. And the ether \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2OCH_3}\) is not oxidised at all under these conditions; ethers are notably resistant.

So the carbon count fixes the skeleton and the oxygen count fixes the class.

rows.stem: On mixing 10 mL of acetone with 50 mL of chloroform, the total volume of the solution will be :
rows.solution:
The total volume is LESS THAN 60 mL.

Acetone and chloroform form a solution with a NEGATIVE deviation from Raoult's law. Neither liquid hydrogen bonds to itself, but mixing them creates a NEW hydrogen bond: the chloroform hydrogen, made acidic by the three chlorines pulling on it, bonds to the lone pair on the acetone oxygen.

The unlike molecules therefore attract one another MORE strongly than the like molecules did. Stronger attraction pulls them closer together, the volume of mixing is negative, and the solution occupies less than the 60 mL of liquid that went in.

The same fact shows up in two other ways: mixing releases heat, and the vapour pressure is lower than Raoult's law predicts.

rows.stem: The unit of cell constant is :
rows.solution:
The unit of cell constant is \(\mathrm{cm^{-1}}\).

The cell constant is the ratio of the ELECTRODE SEPARATION to the ELECTRODE AREA:
\(G^{*} = \dfrac{l}{A}\)
a length divided by an area, which leaves reciprocal length — centimetres to the minus one.

The same answer comes from the relation \(\kappa = G^{*}/R\). Conductivity carries \(\mathrm{S\ cm^{-1}}\) and resistance \(\mathrm{ohm}\), and since siemens is the reciprocal of ohm, the two cancel and only \(\mathrm{cm^{-1}}\) survives.

Of the distractors, \(\mathrm{ohm^{-1}\ cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\) is the unit of MOLAR CONDUCTIVITY — a genuinely different quantity that this question is careful to sit beside.

rows.stem: For a certain reaction \(\mathrm{R} \longrightarrow\) products, a plot of log [R] vs. time gives a straight line with a slope of \(-1{\cdot}25\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}\). The order of the reaction is :
rows.solution:
The order is ONE.

For a first order reaction the integrated rate equation, written with common logarithms, is
\(\log[\mathrm{R}] = \log[\mathrm{R}]_0 - \dfrac{k}{2{\cdot}303}\,t\)

which is a straight line when \(\log[\mathrm{R}]\) is plotted against \(t\). No other order gives a straight line on THESE axes — zero order gives one when \([\mathrm{R}]\) itself is plotted, and second order when \(1/[\mathrm{R}]\) is.

So the shape of this particular plot identifies the order on its own, and the slope then gives the constant: \(k = -2{\cdot}303 \times \text{slope}\).

The unit supplied is a second check. A slope in \(\mathrm{s^{-1}}\) means a rate constant in \(\mathrm{s^{-1}}\), and reciprocal time is the unit of a FIRST order constant specifically.

rows.stem:
For a zero order reaction \(\mathrm{A} \longrightarrow\) products, \(\mathrm{t_{1/2}}\) is :
where \([\mathrm{A}]_0\) = initial concentration of the reactant, k = rate constant.
rows.solution:
For a zero order reaction the half-life is
\(t_{1/2} = \dfrac{[\mathrm{A}]_0}{2k}\)

Derive it rather than recall it. A zero order reaction proceeds at a constant rate, so its integrated equation is
\([\mathrm{A}] = [\mathrm{A}]_0 - kt\)

Half-life is the time at which \([\mathrm{A}] = [\mathrm{A}]_0/2\):
\(\dfrac{[\mathrm{A}]_0}{2} = [\mathrm{A}]_0 - k\,t_{1/2}\)
\(k\,t_{1/2} = \dfrac{[\mathrm{A}]_0}{2}\), so \(t_{1/2} = \dfrac{[\mathrm{A}]_0}{2k}\)

Note that this half-life DOES depend on the starting concentration — it is directly proportional to it, since the reaction is grinding along at a fixed rate and twice as much takes twice as long. That is the opposite of first order, where \(t_{1/2} = 0{\cdot}693/k\) carries no concentration term at all. The option \(2{\cdot}303\log 2/k\) is that first order expression, offered here as the trap.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Aniline is a weaker base than cyclohexylamine.
Reason (R) : Aniline is resonance stabilized.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE - the Assertion prints, in parentheses immediately after the word "cyclohexylamine", a structural gloss of that same compound: a PLAIN hexagon with NO inner double-bond strokes (verified at 5x against the Kekule rings elsewhere in this paper) joined by a single bond to the label "NH2". The compound is already named losslessly in the words of the stem, so the row is answerable from text. Page idx 10.
rows.solution:
Both statements are true, but the Reason is NOT the correct explanation of the Assertion.

Aniline IS the weaker base — \(\mathrm{pK_b}\) about 9.4 against cyclohexylamine's 3.3 — and aniline IS resonance stabilised.

But "resonance stabilised" as stated describes the stability of the MOLECULE, and stability is not by itself a reason for weak basicity. What actually weakens the base is something more specific: the nitrogen's LONE PAIR is delocalised into the ring, so it is not freely available to accept a proton.

The two are close, but the Reason stops one step short of the argument — a molecule can be resonance stabilised without any of that delocalisation touching the group whose basicity is in question. Cyclohexylamine's nitrogen, attached to a saturated ring, keeps its lone pair entirely to itself.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Vitamin C cannot be stored in our body.
Reason (R) : Vitamin C is water soluble and readily excreted in urine.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Both statements are true and the Reason IS the correct explanation of the Assertion.

Vitamin C, ascorbic acid, is WATER SOLUBLE. Any excess taken in dissolves in the body's aqueous fluids and passes straight out in the urine rather than being laid down anywhere — so no reserve accumulates, and a regular dietary supply is required.

That is exactly why it cannot be stored, so the Reason accounts for the Assertion completely.

The contrast is with the FAT-soluble vitamins — A, D, E and K — which are stored in the liver and in adipose tissue and therefore need not be supplied daily. The practical consequence is historical: scurvy appeared on long sea voyages after only a few weeks without fresh food.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Ammonolysis of alkyl halides involves reaction between alkyl halide and ethanolic solution of ammonia.
Reason (R) : Ammonolysis of alkyl halides mainly produces secondary amines.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE.

Ammonolysis does proceed as the Assertion describes — an alkyl halide is heated with an ETHANOLIC or aqueous solution of ammonia in a sealed tube.

But the Reason misstates the product. The reaction does not mainly give SECONDARY amines. It gives a MIXTURE, because the primary amine formed first is itself a better nucleophile than ammonia and goes on to attack more halide, giving the secondary amine, then the tertiary, and finally the quaternary ammonium salt.

Which product dominates is decided by the PROPORTIONS. A large excess of AMMONIA makes any given halide molecule overwhelmingly likely to meet ammonia first, so the PRIMARY amine dominates; an excess of HALIDE drives the sequence to the quaternary salt. Neither condition favours the secondary amine particularly, which is why Gabriel's synthesis is preferred when a pure primary amine is wanted.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Aniline does not undergo Friedel-Crafts reaction.
Reason (R) : Friedel-Crafts reaction is a nucleophilic substitution reaction.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE.

Aniline genuinely does not undergo Friedel-Crafts reaction. The catalyst, aluminium chloride, is a LEWIS ACID, and the nitrogen's lone pair is exactly what it seeks — so it bonds to the nitrogen and is tied up. Worse, the nitrogen is now positively charged, and a positively charged group is strongly deactivating and meta directing, so the ring can barely react at all.

The Reason misnames the reaction type. Friedel-Crafts is an ELECTROPHILIC substitution, not a nucleophilic one: the attacking species is a carbocation or an acylium ion, and the electron-rich benzene ring is what attacks it.

Corrected, the Reason would still not have explained the Assertion — aniline's problem is the catalyst, not the mechanism's classification.

rows.stem:
(a) Which one of the following pairs of substances undergoes \(\mathrm{S_N1}\) reaction faster and why ?
\(\mathrm{CH_3 - CH_2 - CH_2 - Cl}\) OR \(\mathrm{CH_2 = CH - CH_2 - Cl}\)
(b) Write the major product in the following :
\(p\text{-}\mathrm{NO_2 - C_6H_4 - Cl} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{(ii)\ H^{+}}]{\mathrm{(i)\ NaOH,\ 443\ K}} ?\)
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE - in sub-part (b) the substrate is PRINTED AS A DRAWING, not as the condensed formula transcribed above: a KEKULE benzene ring (inner double-bond strokes present, checked at 4x) carrying the label "Cl" at its top vertex and "NO2" at the OPPOSITE (para) vertex, with a reaction arrow labelled "(i) NaOH, 443 K" above and "(ii) H+" below, leading to "?". Sub-part (a) is printed as ordinary condensed formulae and needs no crop. Naming the substrate does not give away the answer, which is the PRODUCT. Page idx 10.
rows.solution:
(a) ALLYL CHLORIDE, \(\mathrm{CH_2{=}CH{-}CH_2{-}Cl}\), reacts faster.

The rate of an \(\mathrm{S_N}1\) reaction is set by how easily the CARBOCATION forms, since that is the slow step. Allyl chloride's halogen sits on the carbon NEXT TO the double bond, so when the chloride leaves the positive charge is delocalised over TWO carbons — two equivalent resonance structures share it:
\(\mathrm{CH_2{=}CH{-}\overset{+}{C}H_2} \longleftrightarrow \mathrm{\overset{+}{C}H_2{-}CH{=}CH_2}\)

n-Propyl chloride gives a plain PRIMARY carbocation with no such help. A more stable intermediate means a lower energy barrier and a faster reaction.

(b) The major product is p-NITROPHENOL.

Chlorobenzene itself needs 623 K and 300 atmospheres to be hydrolysed. Here a NITRO group sits PARA to the chlorine, and it changes everything: it is strongly electron withdrawing, and from the para position it can take the negative charge of the carbanion intermediate right onto its own oxygen by resonance. A stabilised intermediate means a far lower barrier, so 443 K suffices.

\(\mathrm{p\text{-}O_2N{-}C_6H_4{-}Cl} \xrightarrow[2.\ \mathrm{H^+}]{1.\ \mathrm{NaOH},\ 443\ \mathrm{K}} \mathrm{p\text{-}O_2N{-}C_6H_4{-}OH}\)

The position is what does the work: a nitro group at the META position could not accept that charge and would barely help at all.

rows.stem:
Define the following terms :
(a) Peptide linkage
(b) Essential amino acids
rows.solution:
(a) A PEPTIDE LINKAGE is the amide bond \(-\mathrm{CO-NH}-\) that joins two amino acids. The carboxyl group of one condenses with the amino group of the next, a molecule of water is lost, and the bond formed between that carbon and that nitrogen is the peptide linkage.

It is what builds a protein from its residues, and the sequence of those residues — fixed by these bonds — is the protein's primary structure.

(b) ESSENTIAL AMINO ACIDS are those the body CANNOT synthesise for itself; they have to be supplied in the diet. Valine, leucine, isoleucine and lysine are among them.

The contrast is with NON-ESSENTIAL amino acids, such as glycine and alanine, which the body can make. Note that the name describes what the DIET must supply, not how important the acid is — both kinds are needed for protein synthesis, and a protein cannot be built if any one residue is missing.

rows.subtopic: Colligative Properties and Determination of Molar Mass
rows.stem: A 3% solution of glucose (molar mass = 180 g \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\)) is isotonic with \(2{\cdot}5\%\) solution of an unknown organic substance. Calculate the molecular weight of the unknown organic substance.
rows.solution:
ISOTONIC means the two solutions have the SAME osmotic pressure. Since \(\Pi = CRT\) and both are at the same temperature, equal osmotic pressure means equal MOLAR CONCENTRATION:
\(C_1 = C_2\)

Both percentages are mass per unit volume and refer to the same volume, so the concentrations may be compared as mass divided by molar mass:
\(\dfrac{w_1}{M_1} = \dfrac{w_2}{M_2}\)
\(\dfrac{3}{180} = \dfrac{2{\cdot}5}{M_2}\)

\(M_2 = \dfrac{2{\cdot}5 \times 180}{3}\)

\(M_2 = 150\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\)

The result is worth a sanity check: the unknown is present at a SMALLER mass than the glucose yet gives the same number of moles, so its molar mass must be the smaller of the two — and 150 is less than 180, as it should be. Note also that neither answer depends on knowing the temperature, since it cancels from both sides.
